Verdict: REVISEThe central capacity argument in Sections 1–5 is mathematically sound under the natural intended definitions. In particular:arbitrary-length sealed runs really do have capacity at least two;maximal horizontal/vertical runs have tile multiplicity at most two;the resulting inequality holds for every subcollection, so Hall’s theorem gives an actual non-reusing slot allocation;the reservation rule is valid once prior credits are represented by disjoint capacity slots;the weighted replication argument is valid after one missing definition and one missing subset calculation are supplied;the ledger implication is correct and does not imply universal strip coverage.The package as a whole still merits REVISE for two reasons:the optional crossing-owner lemma requires an explicit receiver-set hypothesis that is not among the printed base facts; and  the sharpness example in Section 7 is not self-contained, and the claimed border completion may alter the maximal runs unless additional labels and coordinates are supplied.There is no counterexample to the core Sections 2–5 capacity/Hall theorem under the intended interpretation.1. Preliminary definitions that must be made explicitTwo terms need tightening.First, “selected vertices” in the unit-square argument must mean vertices of  $T$ , not vertices of  $T\cup P$ . The statementEvery unit square contains at most two selected verticesfollows because any three  $T$ -vertices in a  $2\times2$  unit square include one vertex adjacent to the other two, violating the feasibility condition. If “selected” were read as  $T\cup P$ , the statement need not hold: endpoint vertices are not subject to the same three-selected-vertex argument.Second, “blank” must mean an actually blank vertex, namely a vertex carrying neither a  $T$ -label nor a  $P$ -label. The sealed-strip proof uses the fact that no  $T$ -vertex occurs in the two boundary columns. If “blank” meant only “endpoint-free,” the proof would not follow.It is also useful to state explicitly that all runs are deduplicated as geometric maximal intervals. A run and its reversal are one run; the horizontal and vertical singleton descriptions of the same physical tile are two different runs because they are different axis directions.2. Arbitrary-length sealed-strip capacityThis part is correct.For a horizontal run  $s$  of  $k$  physical tiles, the associated vertex rectangle has two rows and  $2k$  vertex columns. If the first and last vertex columns are blank, all  $T$ -vertices lie in the  $2(2k-2)$  interior sites.For  $k\ge 2$ , partition the interior columns into the  $k-1$  shifted  $2\times2$  squares
$$(2,3),\ (4,5),\ \ldots,\ (2k-2,2k-1),$$
where the displayed numbers refer to vertex-column indices. These squares are disjoint and each contains at most two  $T$ -vertices. Hence
$$|T\cap s|\le 2(k-1).$$
Since  $s$  consists of  $k$  endpoint-free physical tiles,
$$\sum_{Q\in s}d_Q
=
2k-|T\cap s|
\ge 2k-2(k-1)=2.$$
For  $k=1$ , both columns of the sole physical tile are blank, so all four vertices are blank and  $d_Q=2$ . The vertical case follows by transposition.The fact that the shifted auxiliary  $2\times2$  squares are not members of the fixed physical tiling causes no problem. They are used only to bound the number of  $T$ -vertices. Their capacities are not separately added to the ledger.Ambient-boundary runs are also harmless for this local lemma: sealing is a condition on the outermost vertex columns or rows that actually exist inside the run.3. Every-subset Hall inequality and actual non-reuseThis is the strongest part of the package, and it is correct.For a run  $s$ , write
$$C_s(d):=\sum_{Q\in s} d_Q.$$
For a collection  $A$  of distinct maximal sealed runs, let  $U(A)$  be the union of their tiles and  $m_A(Q)$  the number of runs in  $A$  containing  $Q$ . Because:distinct horizontal maximal runs are disjoint;distinct vertical maximal runs are disjoint;a horizontal run and a vertical run intersect in at most one tile;one has
$$m_A(Q)\le 2.$$
Therefore
$$\begin{aligned}
2|A|
&\le \sum_{s\in A} C_s(d) \\
&= \sum_{Q\in U(A)}m_A(Q)d_Q \\
&\le 2\sum_{Q\in U(A)}d_Q.
\end{aligned}$$
Thus
$$|A|\le \sum_{Q\in U(A)}d_Q.
\tag{H}$$
Now create  $d_Q$  distinguishable abstract unit slots in each tile  $Q$ . A run  $s$  is adjacent to all slots belonging to its constituent tiles. For a set  $A$  of runs, its slot-neighborhood has cardinality
$$|N(A)|=\sum_{Q\in U(A)}d_Q.$$
Equation (H) is exactly Hall’s condition:
$$|N(A)|\ge |A|
\qquad\text{for every }A.$$
Consequently, there is a matching assigning every run a distinct slot. This handles:horizontal–vertical crossings;the case where two singleton axis-runs share one tile;arbitrary run lengths;capacity-two tiles shared by two runs.It is not merely a global counting argument. The all-subsets quantifier is present, so the matching conclusion is justified.The augmenting-path explanation is also valid. If a new run could not be augmented into an existing matching, the alternating reachable set would produce a set of runs with fewer neighboring slots than runs, contradicting (H).The conclusion
$$|S|\le D$$
is therefore valid for every collection  $S$  of distinct sealed maximal runs. It does not assert that such a collection exists with enough cardinality to cover the receiver charge.4. Reservations and residual capacityThe reservation argument is correct, but one hypothesis should be stated more sharply.A valid reservation consists of actual previously consumed capacity slots. Formally, one should require:
$$a_Q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\qquad
0\le a_Q\le d_Q,\qquad Q\in Z,$$
together with the interpretation that  $a_Q$  is the number of distinct slots already assigned at  $Q$ , with no previously assigned slot reused.Then
$$r_Q=d_Q-a_Q$$
is the number of residual slots at  $Q$ , and
$$\sum_Q r_Q
=
D-\sum_Qa_Q
=
D-B.$$
For a residual run  $s$ , define
$$C_s(r):=\sum_{Q\in s}r_Q.$$
If every selected residual run satisfies
$$C_s(r)\ge 2,$$
then for every subcollection  $A$  of residual runs,
$$\begin{aligned}
2|A|
&\le \sum_{s\in A}C_s(r)\\
&=\sum_{Q\in U(A)}m_A(Q)r_Q\\
&\le2\sum_{Q\in U(A)}r_Q.
\end{aligned}$$
The same Hall argument gives a matching into residual slots, and hence
$$B+|S_{\mathrm{res}}|
\le B+\sum_Qr_Q
=D.$$
The condition that the residual runs remain maximal is still necessary. If one allowed arbitrary nested subintervals after reservation, the same-direction multiplicity could exceed one, and  $m_A(Q)\le2$  would no longer follow.The phrase “each amount assigned at most once” should be replaced by the more precise slot statement. Merely recording a vector  $a_Q$  without certifying that prior credits do not reuse one another is insufficient.Also,  $Q\in Z$  should be stated explicitly. The residual accounting only applies to endpoint-free tiles.5. Weighted extensionThe weighted extension is valid, but the current wording needs a precise definition and an explicit all-subsets calculation.Define the exact residual capacity of each run by
$$C_s:=\sum_{Q\in s}r_Q,$$
and let
$$c_s:=\left\lfloor \frac{C_s}{2}\right\rfloor.$$
Replace  $s$  by  $c_s$  identical unit requests. For an arbitrary set  $Y$  of request copies, let  $A$  be its support, namely the set of runs whose copies occur in  $Y$ . Then
$$|Y|
\le \sum_{s\in A}c_s
\le \frac12\sum_{s\in A}C_s.$$
Using the multiplicity bound,
$$\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s\in A}c_s
&\le \frac12\sum_{Q\in U(A)}m_A(Q)r_Q\\
&\le \sum_{Q\in U(A)}r_Q.
\end{aligned}$$
The neighborhood of  $Y$  is exactly the residual slots in the union  $U(A)$ , so
$$|N(Y)|
=
\sum_{Q\in U(A)}r_Q
\ge |Y|.$$
Thus Hall applies to the request copies.A subtle point should be made explicit: after duplicating runs into request copies, the literal multiplicity of a tile among copies can exceed two. Therefore one should not say that equation (1) is being applied directly to the duplicated collection. The correct argument is the support calculation above, where the multiplicity bound is applied before duplication.If  $C_s$  is intended to be merely an arbitrary lower bound rather than the exact sum  $\sum_{Q\in s}r_Q$ , then the displayed conclusion does not automatically follow. Either define  $C_s$  exactly as above or assume the corresponding subset inequalities separately.6. Ledger consequenceUnder the supplied ledger identity,
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
=
D-\sum_H\rho_H,$$
the cross-component theorem is correct.If
$$\sum_H\rho_H\le B+|S_{\mathrm{res}}|,$$
then the residual Hall allocation gives
$$B+|S_{\mathrm{res}}|\le D.$$
Therefore
$$\sum_H\rho_H\le D,$$
and hence
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|\ge0.$$
Thus
$$|T|+|M|\le\frac{mn}{2}.$$
The positive-part condition is indeed stronger:
$$\sum_H \rho_H
\le
\sum_H\max(\rho_H,0).$$
Consequently,
$$\sum_H\max(\rho_H,0)
\le B+|S_{\mathrm{res}}|$$
implies the required signed inequality.This is a conditional sufficiency theorem. It does not show that enough sealed or residual-capacity runs exist in every representative, and it does not prove
$$\sum_H\rho_H\le B+|S_{\mathrm{res}}|$$
universally. The unrestricted strip-coverage problem remains open exactly as stated.The statement about identifying an optimization value also requires the relevant external lower-bound theorem. It does not follow from this package alone.7. Optional crossing-owner lemmaConditional validityThe planar argument is sound under the standard receiver convention
$$R_H=\{\text{physical tiles containing an endpoint of component }H\},$$
so that
$$Z=V(G)\setminus\bigcup_HR_H,$$
where  $G$  is the tile-center grid.Under that convention, let the horizontal enclosed run be
$$A,q_1,\ldots,q_k,B,$$
with  $A,B\in R_H$  the immediate bounding tiles and  $q_i\in Z$ . Let a perpendicular enclosed run be
$$C,p_1,\ldots,p_\ell,D,$$
with  $C,D\in R_K$ , and suppose the runs share the tile  $q$ .Because  $R_H$  is connected in the tile-center graph, choose a simple  $R_H$ -path  $P$  from  $A$  to  $B$ . Since  $P\subseteq R_H$  and the interior run tiles lie in  $Z$ ,  $P$  is disjoint from the interior of the horizontal run. The union of  $P$  and the straight horizontal path
$$A,q_1,\ldots,q_k,B$$
is therefore a simple cycle in the planar tile-center embedding.The extended vertical path
$$C,p_1,\ldots,p_\ell,D$$
meets the cycle only at  $q$ , because:its interior tiles are in  $Z$ ;the horizontal and vertical runs have only the common tile  $q$ ; $C,D\in R_K$ , so  $C,D\notin R_H$  by disjointness of receiver sets;the square-lattice center embedding has no edge crossings except at common vertices.The common tile  $q$  is an interior point of both straight segments, so the vertical path crosses the cycle transversely there. Hence  $C$  and  $D$  lie on opposite sides of the cycle.But  $R_K$  is connected, so it contains a path from  $C$  to  $D$ . That path is disjoint from the cycle because  $R_K\cap R_H=\varnothing$  and  $R_K\cap Z=\varnothing$ . This contradicts the Jordan separation property. Therefore  $H=K$ .Singleton runs are covered: after adding their two immediate bounding receiver tiles, the shared singleton tile is still an interior point of the corresponding straight segment. Runs touching the ambient boundary are simply not enclosed, because they lack one of the two immediate receiver bounds.Missing hypothesis in the printed packageThe listed base facts state only that different receiver sets are disjoint and connected. They do not explicitly state that receiver tiles are exactly endpoint-bearing tiles, or at least that
$$R_H\cap Z=\varnothing
\qquad\text{for every }H.$$
That condition is used critically in the sentence:the interior run tiles contain no endpoints and cannot occur on the  $R_H$  path.Endpoint-free does not by itself prevent a tile from belonging to a broader receiver neighborhood. If receiver sets were allowed to contain endpoint-free padding tiles, an  $R_H$ -path could run through the horizontal strip, the proposed union might fail to be a simple cycle, and the vertical  $K$ -path could have additional intersections with it. Thus connectedness and pairwise disjointness alone do not prove the owner lemma.The sentenceits  $K$  endpoints are outside  $R_H$ , so no further intersection is possibleis also insufficient as written. Being outside  $R_H$  does not by itself mean being outside the full cycle. The proof must use the stronger facts that the  $K$ -bounding tiles are in  $R_K$ , the interior vertical tiles are in  $Z$ , and the horizontal and vertical  $Z$ -runs intersect only at the common tile.Therefore:if the prior theory already defines  $R_H$  as exactly the tiles meeting endpoints of  $H$ , the crossing-owner lemma is essentially correct after these details are written explicitly;based only on the hypotheses printed in this package, the lemma has a genuine omitted premise.The subsequent statement about disjoint pools of different owners then follows, once the corrected owner lemma is available. A per-component allocation also implicitly requires  $\rho_H$  to be a nonnegative integer when one says that  $H$  has “at least  $\rho_H$  strips.” In the usual matching-component setting  $|H|$  is even, so this is likely automatic, but it should be stated or inherited explicitly.8. Section 7 sharpness exampleThe overlap-sharpness calculation is plausible, but it is not verifiable from the text alone.To certify the example, one needs the exact coordinates and labels, or a prior lemma that supplies them, showing all of the following: $Q_{(3,1)},Q_{(3,2)},Q_{(3,3)},Q_{(2,2)}\in Z$ ;the horizontal and vertical intervals are actually maximal  $Z$ -runs;the two boundary columns of the horizontal run and the two boundary rows of the vertical run are genuinely blank; $d_{(3,2)}=2$  and  $d_{(3,1)}=d_{(3,3)}=d_{(2,2)}=0$ ;every other endpoint-free tile has zero capacity;the feasibility and frozen hypotheses hold;the claimed component charge  $\rho_H=1$  and any other component charges are correct.The “selected-border completion” requires a separate check. Since  $Z$  is defined by absence of endpoints, adding  $T$ -vertices to neighboring tiles does not by itself make those tiles leave  $Z$ . Such a completion could extend a maximal  $Z$ -run or change its sealing. To preserve the listed maximal runs, the newly added neighboring tiles must become non- $Z$ , usually by acquiring endpoint labels, or this must be proved from the actual construction.The phrasethe original uncompleted example supplies equality for the total budgetshould also be made precise. The displayed data establish, at most,
$$|S|=D=2,$$
which is equality for the one-unit overlap/Hall budget. They do not by themselves establish equality in the full ledger
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|=D-\sum_H\rho_H.$$
If “total budget” means the capacity budget  $D$ , say so. If it means equality in the final grid bound, the complete charge data are required.Once the coordinates and completion proof are supplied, the example does correctly show that assigning two credits independently to each overlapping strip is invalid: the two strips have total nominal strip capacity four, while the union has only two actual slots in the shared tile.9. Verification sectionThe finite scanner cases and the six local Lean statements do not repair any of the written gaps, but the package is appropriately careful to say that they do not formalize:full maximal-run classification;the double-counting adapter;the planar owner argument;the Hall allocation itself.No objection arises from the fact that the controls are not being treated as proofs.Required revisionsTo turn the package into an acceptable theorem note, I would require these edits:Replace “selected vertices” by “ $T$ -vertices” in the unit-square bound.Define “blank” explicitly as the  $B$ -label.State that all reservations are on  $Z$ , are integral, and correspond to already consumed distinct slots.Define the weighted quantity explicitly by
$$C_s=\sum_{Q\in s}r_Q.$$
Give the weighted Hall inequality for every support subset, not only for the full collection.State the receiver convention
$$R_H=\{\text{tiles containing endpoints of }H\},
\qquad
Z=V(G)\setminus\bigcup_HR_H,$$
or at minimum  $R_H\cap Z=\varnothing$ .State that the owner proof takes place in the planar square-lattice embedding of the tile-center graph.Replace the “outside  $R_H$ , so no further intersection” sentence by the full unique-intersection argument.Supply exact data or a cited prior lemma for the Section 7 frozen configuration and prove that the border completion preserves maximality, sealing, and capacities.Clarify whether the claimed sharp equality in Section 7 is equality for the capacity budget or equality in the full ledger.With those repairs, Sections 1–5 and the cross-component compensation theorem should be accepted as a correct conditional capacity theorem. The theorem still makes no claim of universal strip coverage, and nothing in the Hall argument closes that open problem.
